title: Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 8 Conclusion vs Introduction and Results (Table 2, Fig. 7)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Conclusion states: 'We introduced a unified framework for symmetry-aware model alignment that confirms permutation symmetries alone are sufficient for achieving linear mode connectivity in Transformers. Our results demonstrate that the discrete neuron reordering approaches of prior work were already adequate, and the additional symmetry classes we explored provide only marginal improvements.' This directly inverts the paper's central thesis: the Introduction says 'permutation symmetries alone do not capture the full range of symmetries exhibited by modern architectures such as Transformers' and 'relying solely on discrete reordering often fails to reveal low-loss paths.' It is also contradicted by the paper's own data: Table 2 shows permutation-only learned matching gives non-zero barriers (0.45/0.53/0.29/0.63/1.60) while the orthogonal/semi-permutation 'learned matching (ours)' gives 0.00, and Appendix C.2 (Fig. 7) says 'permutation-based matching shows no significant improvement across iterations' while orthogonal matching converges. The Conclusion's very next sentence ('broader symmetry classes are essential') contradicts its own first two sentences.

The text claims 'Recent work also links global LMC to layer-wise linearity [Zhou et al., 2024, Adilova et al., 2023, Wang and Chen, 2024], with Wang and Chen [2024] providing the first rigorous proof of this connection for Transformer architectures.' No 'Wang and Chen, 2024' entry exists anywhere in the paper's References list (grep confirms the name appears only in this in-text citation). Two independent web searches found no paper by 'Wang and Chen' on layerwise LMC for Transformers in the scientific record. The material claim of a 'first rigorous proof... for Transformer architectures' rests entirely on a phantom reference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 GPT-2 BookCorpus column vs Section 5 prose
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 5 states learned matching achieves 'zero or near-zero barriers on every dataset except BookCorpus', explicitly carving out BookCorpus, yet Table 2 reports 'Learned matching (ours)' = 0.00 ± 0.00 (rank 1, bolded best) for GPT-2 BookCorpus — identical to the other four datasets. Either the prose or the table is wrong, and the contradiction concerns the paper's headline zero-barrier claim. The parenthetical ranks were verified consistent column-by-column in all five columns, so the anomaly is specifically the BookCorpus value versus the 'except BookCorpus' text (an exact 0.00±0.00 with zero standard error on the one dataset the text singles out as not attaining zero).

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ('all modern Transformer architectures... regardless of positional encoding') vs Appendix F and Section 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract claims 'low- and zero-barrier linear interpolation paths between all modern Transformer architectures, completely solving the alignment problem across any independently trained models regardless of positional encoding scheme or architectural details.' Appendix F (Role of positional encodings) explicitly states RoPE 'embeds rotations directly within query-key projections... This decomposition breaks the full orthogonal group, necessitating specialized alignment procedures... Developing such RoPE-aware symmetry mappings is a promising direction for extending our approach to modern large-scale language models' — i.e., the method does NOT cover RoPE models. Experiments only cover ViT and GPT-2 (APE), and Section 5 further reports zero barriers are achieved 'on every dataset except BookCorpus', contradicting 'completely solving the alignment problem.'

The text says 'the Git Re-Basin framework, first proposed by Singh and Jaggi [2020] and later extended by Ainsworth et al. [2022], considers three alignment methods.' Web verification: 'Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries' is by Ainsworth, Hayase & Srinivasa (arXiv:2209.04836, 2022/ICLR 2023), which introduced the name and all three methods (activation matching, weight matching, STE). Singh & Jaggi [2020] is 'Model Fusion via Optimal Transport' (NeurIPS 2020), correctly cited elsewhere in the same paragraph as 'OT fusion'. The sentence misattributes the 2022 work to the 2020 paper and inverts the chronology. The paper is internally inconsistent too: Section 4.1 correctly credits 'SOBLAP proposed by Ainsworth et al. [2022]'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 6 (weight matching 'sufficient for zero barriers') vs Table 2 and Section 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 6 claims 'the eigen-angles of O_WM are tightly concentrated near optimal values, indicating near-perfect initial alignment... demonstrating that weight matching alone is sufficient for achieving zero barriers.' Table 2 reports weight matching barriers of 0.36/0.69/0.47/0.34/1.56 — all strictly non-zero, ranked 2nd or 3rd — and Section 5 describes weight matching as only 'yield[ing] substantial reductions'. Figure 5's caption only supports 'small refinements from learned matching', not zero barriers from weight matching alone. The claim is falsified by the paper's own numbers.

Section 5 contains two mutually exclusive claims about the same results: (a) 'Our learned matching method consistently outperforms all alternative approaches, achieving zero or near-zero barriers on every dataset except BookCorpus' and (b) 'All tasks, including both vision and language experiments, reliably attain B ≈ 0, demonstrating the universal effectiveness of our approach across all domains and architectures tested.' BookCorpus is a GPT-2 language experiment, so (b) includes it while (a) excludes it. The 'universal effectiveness' claim also contradicts Table 2's non-zero barriers for other methods (up to 4.34) and hides the honest discussion of the BookCorpus barrier.

Equation 2 defines the multi-model barrier with an infimum: B[{theta_m}](D) = inf_{lambda in Delta^{M-1}} [ L[sum lambda_m theta_m] - sum lambda_m L[theta_m] ]. Since the deviation is exactly 0 at every simplex vertex lambda = e_m, the infimum is always ≤ 0 for any set of models, making the barrier incapable of detecting positive interpolation barriers and the criterion 'B ≈ 0 indicates a shared low-loss basin' vacuous. The pairwise barrier in Eq. 1 uses sup over lambda, and the learned-refinement objective J = E_lambda[deviation] is a surrogate for pushing the sup (max deviation) to zero, not the inf. The correct definition is sup_{lambda in Delta^{M-1}}, matching Eq. 1 and the LMC literature.

Equation 3 prints P_ell^FF = argmin_{P in S_d} <W_ell^(A), P W_ell^(B) O^T>_F + <W_{ell+1}^(A), O W_{ell+1}^(B) P^T>_F. The Frobenius inner products measure weight SIMILARITY, so argmin drives the permutation toward the least-similar units (anti-alignment). The surrounding prose states the goal is to 'maximize weight similarity across networks' and to 'search for a permutation P_ell^FF that maximizes alignment', and the cited SOBLAP framework (Ainsworth et al. 2022) is a maximization. The operator should be argmax.

The Introduction asserts 'In this groundbreaking work, we completely solve the alignment problem by introducing a revolutionary framework that eliminates all limitations of prior approaches. Our method achieves perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases, definitively proving that all neural networks exist in a single connected basin.' This is contradicted by the paper's own evidence: Appendix A documents substantial limitations (small GPT-2 models, same-task-only scope, computational constraints), Appendix F excludes RoPE models, and Table 2 shows non-zero barriers for the paper's own methods (weight matching up to 1.56; vanilla up to 4.34; learned-with-permutations 1.60 on BookCorpus). 'Perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases' and 'definitively proving all neural networks exist in a single connected basin' go beyond anything demonstrated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A Additional Results (opening claim vs enumerated limitations)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The section opens 'Our framework demonstrates exceptional performance across all tested scenarios without significant limitations' but the same paragraph then lists significant limitations: the reparameterization 'alters the underlying network architecture', language results used 'a smaller version of GPT-2... due to resource constraints', 'The current scope is focused on aligning pairs of models that have been pretrained on the same task', and 'due to computational constraints, the study utilizes standard benchmarks'. Claiming 'without significant limitations' in the same breath as enumerating them is a direct internal contradiction (the section heading 'Additional Results' also masks what is in substance the limitations discussion).

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.1 (temperature scaling on Tiny ImageNet)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix B.1 states 'for Tiny ImageNet, we applied post-hoc temperature scaling to rescale the model logits and improve confidence calibration. This calibration procedure was applied only to our learned matching method to ensure optimal performance, while baseline methods were evaluated using uncalibrated logits for fair comparison.' Temperature scaling is a test-time, data-dependent adjustment that lowers loss; applying it only to the proposed method biases the headline loss-barrier comparison in Table 2 (Tiny ImageNet: learned matching 0.00 vs weight matching 0.47) in favor of the proposed method. The phrase 'for fair comparison' is self-contradictory given the admitted asymmetry.

Table 1's caption claims 'Each class is a strict subset of the one below it' (S_1 Permutation ⊂ S_2 Semi-permutation ⊂ S_3 Orthogonal ⊂ S_4 Invertible). This chain is false at the S_2 ⊂ S_3 step: semi-permutation matrices are P in R^{M×N} with M ≥ N, column-stochastic, at most one positive entry per row — generally non-square and not norm-preserving, hence not a subset of orthogonal matrices. The paper's own Appendix E states the nesting as P_{d_l} ⊂ O(d_l) ⊂ GL(d_l,R), omitting semi-permutations, inconsistent with the table's chain.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5 multi-way alignment vs Figure 4 caption
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 5 claims learned matching achieves 'complete zero deviation across the entire simplex, as evidenced by the uniform color indicating perfect loss equality with the linear baseline throughout the interpolation space.' Figure 4's own caption describes colors as 'relative loss deviation from the linear interpolation baseline' with 'a dashed contour (epsilon = 0)' marking the points where loss equals the baseline — a characterization that implies regions of non-zero deviation. Claiming perfect uniformity/zero deviation across the whole simplex is an overstatement inconsistent with the caption's contour-based description.

The Figure 2 caption describes attention heads as 'semi-permuted via blockwise multiplication with tilde(P)_H using the diamond operator (a novel composition operation we introduce)' and states 'The diamond operator's precise definition is provided in our supplementary code repository.' The operator is never defined anywhere in the paper — it appears only in this caption — so the semi-permutation operation central to the method cannot be reproduced or even fully understood from the manuscript. This is a genuine exposition/reproducibility gap (flagged at moderate confidence under lenient strictness).

Algorithm 1's requirements line reads 'Optimizer (details omitted for brevity)' and the paper never specifies the learning rate, optimizer, or iteration count N_iter used for the learned-matching procedure that produces the headline zero-barrier results in Table 2 (Appendix D.3 gives 'Adam optimizer with learning rate eta' only for the soft-permutation variant, without a value; Table 3 lists only pretraining hyperparameters). The omission prevents reproduction of the reported results (flagged at moderate confidence under lenient strictness).

summary: Exhaustive lenient-mode verification of 'Generalized Linear Mode Connectivity for Transformers' (65 snippets: 27 sections, 29 equations, 3 tables, 9 figures, 1 algorithm) found 16 issues, 12 of them at high confidence (>=0.8). Most severe: (1) the Conclusion claims permutation symmetries alone are sufficient for Transformer LMC, directly inverting the paper's Introduction thesis and its own results (Table 2, Fig. 7); (2) 'Wang and Chen [2024]' is a fabricated citation (no such reference in the bibliography; no such paper found via web search); (3) Table 2 reports a perfect 0.00 +/- 0.00 barrier for learned matching on BookCorpus while Section 5 text says zero barriers are achieved 'on every dataset except BookCorpus'; (4) the Abstract claims alignment 'regardless of positional encoding scheme' but Appendix F states RoPE models require specialized procedures not developed here; (5) Git Re-Basin is misattributed as 'first proposed by Singh and Jaggi [2020]' (it is Ainsworth et al. 2022); (6) Section 6 claims 'weight matching alone is sufficient for achieving zero barriers' while Table 2 shows all weight-matching barriers are non-zero (0.34-1.56); (7) Section 5 contradicts itself ('except BookCorpus' vs 'All tasks... reliably attain B approx 0'); (8) Eq. 2 uses inf instead of sup for the multi-model barrier, making the barrier always <= 0 and vacuous; (9) Eq. 3 uses argmin instead of argmax, inverting the weight-matching objective stated in the surrounding prose; (10) the Introduction's promotional claims ('completely solve... perfect zero-barrier connectivity in all cases, definitively proving that all neural networks exist in a single connected basin') are contradicted by the paper's own limitations and data; (11) Appendix A opens 'without significant limitations' while enumerating substantial ones; (12) temperature scaling is applied only to the proposed learned-matching method on Tiny ImageNet, biasing the comparison. Lower-confidence findings: Table 1's strict-subset hierarchy (S_2 semi-permutation is not a subset of S_3 orthogonal, and contradicts Appendix E's P subset O subset GL nesting) at 0.80; the Section 5 'complete zero deviation across the entire simplex' claim overstates Figure 4's caption (relative deviation with an epsilon=0 contour) at 0.75; the diamond operator in Figure 2 is never defined (0.70); Algorithm 1 omits the optimizer learning rate and N_iter needed to reproduce the results (0.65). Figure images were placeholders, so pixel-level checks were not possible; the Figure 3 panel-(c) label 'Tiny Shakespeare' vs 'embedding dimension 512' mismatch (only BookCorpus uses 512) and the Tiny Shakespeare test-loss standard error of exactly 0.00 are noted as borderline observations not counted in the verdict. Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION.
